title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow

paper.title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow
paper.abstract: Abstract Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Early stopping is a standard mechanism used to prevent overfitting, in particular in the presence of label noise. The usual dynamical picture is that training first learns structure shared across examples and only later fits labels that cannot be predicted from the inputs. Continued training then degrades test performance, so the best generalization error is attained at a finite time, before interpolation. This intuition is made precise in theoretical analyses of linear, kernel, and neural-network dynamics, where early stopping acts as an implicit regularizer that prevents the learner from fitting corrupted labels ( Yao et al., 2007 ; Raskutti et al., 2014 ; Ali et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2020 ) . One might therefore expect early stopping to be particularly important when an extensive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable. We challenge this expectation through a controlled experiment based on CIFAR10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) . Cats and dogs define a shared classification task, while automobile images, comprising 20% of the training set, receive fixed random labels. We measure the generalization error on new samples of cats and dogs and the memorization error, defined as the fraction of misclassified automobiles in the training set, to track when the unpredictable labels have been fitted. Figure 1 follows the two errors jointly as training progresses across architectures and model sizes. Fixed-feature and smaller or shallower models exhibit the familiar behavior: as the memorization error decreases, the test performance eventually deteriorates. For the larger, deeper convolutional and residual networks, this deterioration is essentially absent: their best observed test performance is attained with zero memorization error, and early stopping does not visibly improve generalization. Empirical hypothesis. In image classification, even with extensive label noise, large, deep neural networks with competitive test performance do not benefit from early stopping. Appendix F examines this empirical hypothesis in more detail. We report the unsmoothed neural network trajectories and training losses behind Figure 1 , together with additional convolutional and residual architectures. We also consider other training procedures commonly used to obtain stronger performance on image-classification tasks, combining cross-entropy loss, data augmentation, learning-rate warm-up and cosine decay, followed by an extended constant-rate tail. We also replace the automobiles by randomly labelled cats and dogs, so that clean and randomized examples belong to the same image classes. The evidence collected in Appendix F robustly points to the same qualitative behavior: the larger and more complex networks attain their best observed test performance after all random labels have been classified correctly, with little subsequent deterioration. Further controls examine the effects of the optimizer, batch size, training-set size and fraction of random labels. This raises the theoretical question of whether there are settings in which one can show analytically that training all the way to interpolation gives the lowest test error. This question is related to, but distinct from, grokking and benign overfitting. Canonical grokking concerns noiseless, realizable tasks, where training accuracy becomes essentially perfect long before test performance improves ( Power et al., 2022 ) . Here, instead, a considerable fraction of the labels is intrinsically unpredictable, and we ask whether fitting them eventually harms generalization. Benign overfitting asks whether an interpolating estimator can generalize well despite label noise ( Bartlett et al., 2020 ; Liang and Rakhlin, 2020 ) ; it does not by itself determine whether interpolation is optimal relative to earlier points along the training trajectory. Our focus is precisely on this dynamical comparison between early stopping and convergence. Can the minimum test error nevertheless genuinely occur at convergence? Existing theoretical analyses that follow feature-learning dynamics under label noise toward interpolation reach the opposite conclusion for the shallow neural networks they study in the regimes analyzed: fitting the noisy labels eventually degrades generalization, making early stopping preferable ( Han et al., 2025 ; Montanari and Urbani, 2025 ) . They therefore do not account for the empirical hypothesis formulated here. We show that such behavior is possible for square-loss kernel gradient flow in the Rules-and-Facts (RAF) model introduced by Farné et al. (2026) . Each training label either follows a shared linear rule or is independent of the input. Whereas Farné et al. (2026) analyze the resulting empirical risk minimizers (ERM) under explicit regularization, here we follow the full learning trajectory from initialization to interpolation in the absence of explicit regularization. In the proportional high-dimensional limit, this trajectory is governed by the relative strengths of the rule-aligned component and the higher-order kernel components that provide the capacity to fit the unpredictable labels.

sections.heading: Main theoretical result.
sections.text: We derive exact learning curves and obtain a phase diagram with three regimes, corresponding to three families of kernels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. Thus, even in the presence of extensive label noise, interpolation can lead to a better test error than any early stopping. The kernel analysis therefore produces the behavior that motivated this work. At the critical geometry, the best test error is attained at interpolation, and the corresponding trajectory in Figure 4 closely resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 , whose best test performance is attained after all randomly labelled examples have been classified correctly. The theory thus provides a concrete realization of the observed phenomenon. It does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. Determining which aspects of feature learning, model size, and architecture produce this behavior remains an open question.

sections.heading: Learning with label noise.
sections.text: Deep networks can fit arbitrary random labels ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , while often learning shared structure before memorizing individual samples ( Arpit et al., 2017 ) . This separation of time scales motivates early stopping as a method for improving robustness to label noise ( Li et al., 2020 ; Bai et al., 2021 ) . The severity of late-time overfitting, however, depends on model capacity and optimization, as illustrated by epoch-wise double descent ( Nakkiran et al., 2021 ; Heckel and Yilmaz, 2021 ) and by the weak overtraining observed in sufficiently overparameterized models ( Advani et al., 2020 ) . These works do not provide an exact criterion for when fitting the remaining label noise ceases to harm generalization.

sections.heading: Early stopping and learning trajectories.
sections.text: For least squares, early stopping acts as a spectral regularizer ( Yao et al., 2007 ; Raskutti et al., 2014 ) , and the complete gradient-flow trajectory has an explicit matrix-exponential form ( Ali et al., 2019 ) . High-dimensional learning curves have been derived for linear, kernel, and Gaussian-covariate models ( Advani et al., 2020 ; Ghosh et al., 2022 ; Bodin and Macris, 2022 ) , including regimes in which training error decreases while test error remains essentially unchanged ( Ghosh et al., 2022 ) . Recent work also interprets early stopping through a transient spectral transition in an anisotropic linear model ( Coeurdoux et al., 2026 ) . These analyses do not characterize the transition between lowest test error at finite time and at convergence across kernels.

sections.heading: Early stopping and explicit regularization.
sections.text: Early stopping, Tikhonov regularization and other spectral filters can attain comparable statistical rates ( Bauer et al., 2007 ; Yao et al., 2007 ; Raskutti et al., 2014 ; Celisse and Wahl, 2021 ; Hu and Lei, 2022 ) . For least-squares regression, Ali et al. (2019) compare gradient flow with ridge regression under the calibration λ ≍ 1 / t \lambda\asymp 1/t and obtain uniform constant-factor risk comparisons. More recent work shows that a finitely stopped gradient-descent iterate can be represented as a generalized, spectrally dependent ridge solution ( Sonthalia et al., 2024 ) , while high-dimensional and finite-sample comparisons demonstrate that optimally stopped gradient descent and optimally tuned scalar ridge need not attain the same risk ( Stark and Steinberger, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . Our setting makes this distinction fully explicit for classification error.

sections.heading: Benign overfitting and kernel geometry.
sections.text: Benign-overfitting theory characterizes when an interpolating estimator can generalize well despite label noise ( Bartlett et al., 2020 ; Liang and Rakhlin, 2020 ) . More generally, kernel spectra and their alignment with the target control generalization ( Bordelon et al., 2020 ; Canatar et al., 2021 ; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2022 ) , while high-dimensional kernel linearization makes this dependence explicit for broad kernel families ( El Karoui, 2010 ; Do and Vu, 2013 ) . The RAF model provides a characterization of how kernel geometry allocates capacity between rule learning and fitting unpredictable labels ( Farné et al., 2026 ) . These results do not compare full learning trajectories across kernel geometries to determine when the test error at interpolation is lower than at every finite stopping time.

sections.heading: Three geometries, three generalization–memorization paths.
sections.text: Figure 4 displays the analytical trajectories in the same coordinates as the neural-network trajectories in Figure 1 . The data distribution, sample ratio, and initialization are fixed, while we vary the kernel angle γ \gamma . We distinguish three regimes, corresponding to the following kernel families. • Rule-dominated kernels, γ > γ c ​ ( ε ) \gamma>\gamma_{\rm c}(\varepsilon) , generalization initially improves but eventually deteriorates as the randomly labelled examples are fitted, producing a finite optimal stopping time. • Fact-dominated kernels, γ < γ c ​ ( ε ) \gamma<\gamma_{\rm c}(\varepsilon) , the generalization error continues to decrease until interpolation, but the resulting predictor remains suboptimal relative to the critical kernel. • Optimal kernels, γ = γ c ​ ( ε ) \gamma=\gamma_{\rm c}(\varepsilon) : the trajectory reaches the lowest (among all considered kernels and stopping times) test error at the interpolating endpoint, where the memorization error vanishes. Thus, eliminating the benefit of early stopping is not sufficient: optimality is attained specifically at the boundary between the finite-time and interpolation-optimal regimes. All three kernel families have enough capacity to eventually interpolate the training data. What differs is how fitting the unpredictable labels affects predictions on new examples. The critical geometry provides a fixed-representation mechanism through which interpolation can be completed without sacrificing the best generalization attainable within the kernel family. The kernel analysis does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we asked whether the presence of extensive label noise necessarily makes early stopping preferable to interpolation. The noisy CIFAR10 experiments in Fig. 1 and Appendix F support the hypothesis that deep and highly overparameterized neural networks actually do not benefit from early stopping. Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration. Appendix F shows that this observation is robust beyond the setting of Fig. 1 : it persists across a range of training recipes, including cross-entropy, data augmentation, and a scheduled learning rate, as well as across additional optimization controls. We then asked whether the absence of a benefit from early stopping can be reproduced in an analytically solvable setting. Our analysis of high-dimensional learning curves for kernel gradient flow shows that it can. Kernel geometry determines whether the lowest test error occurs at a finite time or at convergence. We identify a critical kernel geometry for which the interpolating predictor attains the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, fitting unpredictable labels need not come at the expense of generalization, in a sense yet considerably stronger than the one known from the literature on benign overfitting. The critical-kernel trajectory provides a concrete fixed-representation counterpart of the behavior observed in the deeper neural networks: fitting the unpredictable labels does not produce a late-time deterioration of generalization, and the best test error is attained at the end of the trajectory. Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior. The theory nevertheless places the empirical hypothesis formulated in the introduction on a precise footing: even under extensive label noise, the absence of a benefit from early stopping is possible and can be controlled by representation geometry. Understanding how larger and deeper feature-learning architectures realize analogous behavior remains an open question. All the results can be reproduced using the code provided in the repository: https://github.com/SPOC-group/Early-stopping .

sections.heading: Appendix E Numerical checks and kernel experiments
sections.text: In this section, we test our theoretical predictions in the previous appendix sections and in the main text against numerical simulations in several different learning regimes. We first compare the predicted generalization and memorization curves with the dynamics of a full nonlinear RBF kernel on synthetic RAF data. We then move to the CIFAR10 dataset construction of the main text, namely with cat/dogs images preserving their true labels (to generalize on) and randomized automobiles (to memorize), and examine whether changing the kernel produces qualitatively similar behavior on real image data.

sections.heading: Appendix F Neural-network experiments on CIFAR10
sections.text: In this section we describe the experiments behind Figure 1 and examine how the observation varies with the training recipe used. The question is whether fitting the unpredictable labels in the dataset necessarily increases the test error on new cats and dogs with their original labels. We first report the square-loss protocol and unsmoothed network trajectories including the training loss, so as to complement Figure 1 . We then consider augmented cross-entropy training and additional optimizer and residual-network controls. We also randomize labels on cats and dogs themselves, and vary the optimizer, sample size, batch size and random-label fraction. All these experiments compare finite training trajectories.

sections.heading: F.1 Data, observables and square-loss training
sections.text: Following the CIFAR10 dataset construction of Farné et al. (2026) , the dataset in Figure 1 contains 2800 2800 cats labelled + 1 +1 , 2800 2800 dogs labelled − 1 -1 , and 1400 1400 automobiles assigned independent uniform labels in { − 1 , + 1 } \{-1,+1\} . The first two models have the form f ⁡ ( x ) = v ⊤ ​ ϕ F ​ ( x ) + c f(x)=v^{\top}\phi_{F}(x)+c , where F F denotes the convolutional weights. The feature map ϕ F \phi_{F} applies average pooling, a 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution with rectified linear activation (ReLU), spatial averaging, and a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution with ReLU. The four- and six-layer CNNs use blocks comprising a convolution, batch normalization and ReLU, followed by global average pooling, layer normalization and an affine output. sections.heading: F.2 Augmented cross-entropy training
sections.text: We next ask whether the same observation persists under a training recipe commonly used to obtain good test performance on CIFAR10: cross-entropy, random crops and horizontal flips, and a scheduled learning rate ( Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2016 ; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ; He et al., 2019 ) . We use a separate fixed dataset containing 2458 2458 cats, 2458 2458 dogs and 1228 1228 randomly labelled automobiles ( n = 6144 n=6144 ), with five training seeds and the same 2000 2000 official-test cats and dogs. Inputs are standardized using this dataset’s training statistics. 4-layer CNN, 6-layer CNN, ResNet-16, WRN-28 and MobileNetV2 each have approximately 2.7 2.7 million optimized parameters. Here, the model labelled ResNet-16 is the wide residual architecture WRN-16-4: the width multiplier four gives 64 64 , 128 128 and 256 256 channels in its three residual groups. MobileNetV2 is a computationally efficient convolutional architecture that combines convolutions acting separately on each channel with 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolutions that mix channels ( Sandler et al., 2018 ) . We adapt its first convolution to preserve the spatial resolution of the small CIFAR10 images, using stride one, and replace its classifier with a scalar output. All models are trained from scratch. Each epoch presents one randomly transformed view of every training image: four-pixel zero padding, a random 32 × 32 32\times 32 crop and a horizontal flip with probability 1 / 2 1/2 . Although the attained test errors differ across architectures, continued training preserves performance close to the best observed level, with only small fluctuations and little visible advantage from early stopping. Thus, even under this recipe, completing factual memorization does not lead to a substantial deterioration in generalization. The continued decrease in cross-entropy reflects increasing classification margins after the random labels have already been classified correctly. A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow Fabrizio Boncoraglio Lenka Zdeborová 1 Statistical Physics of Computation Laboratory, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) CH-1015 Lausanne Abstract Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry. Figure 1: Generalization along the path to memorization. Test error on 2000 cats and dogs ( x x -axes) versus classification error on the randomly labelled automobiles ( y y -axes) taken from the CIFAR10 dataset. The fixed training set has n = 7000 n=7000 images: 2800 2800 cats, 2800 2800 dogs with their respective labels, and 1400 1400 automobiles with independent random labels. Panels vary the overparametrization ratio κ = P / n ≈ 1 , 10 , 100 \kappa=P/n\approx 1,10,100 , where P P counts optimized parameters. Curves average about 30 completed seeds; a centered arithmetic average of up to seven neighboring recorded times is applied to both coordinates for display, preserving the initial and final values. These parametric curves trace the two errors as training time t t increases. Triangles mark initialization, squares the last iterate and crosses the minimum displayed test error. All trainable networks use square loss and constant-rate Nesterov SGD, without augmentation or weight decay, through 1500 epochs; RF-CNN uses full-batch readout GD through 10 12 10^{12} steps. In Appendix F we provide all numerical details and the unsmoothed trajectories, including training loss. 1 Introduction Early stopping is a standard mechanism used to prevent overfitting, in particular in the presence of label noise. The usual dynamical picture is that training first learns structure shared across examples and only later fits labels that cannot be predicted from the inputs. Continued training then degrades test performance, so the best generalization error is attained at a finite time, before interpolation. This intuition is made precise in theoretical analyses of linear, kernel, and neural-network dynamics, where early stopping acts as an implicit regularizer that prevents the learner from fitting corrupted labels ( Yao et al., 2007 ; Raskutti et al., 2014 ; Ali et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2020 ) . One might therefore expect early stopping to be particularly important when an extensive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable. We challenge this expectation through a controlled experiment based on CIFAR10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) . Cats and dogs define a shared classification task, while automobile images, comprising 20% of the training set, receive fixed random labels. We measure the generalization error on new samples of cats and dogs and the memorization error, defined as the fraction of misclassified automobiles in the training set, to track when the unpredictable labels have been fitted. Figure 1 follows the two errors jointly as training progresses across architectures and model sizes. Fixed-feature and smaller or shallower models exhibit the familiar behavior: as the memorization error decreases, the test performance eventually deteriorates. For the larger, deeper convolutional and residual networks, this deterioration is essentially absent: their best observed test performance is attained with zero memorization error, and early stopping does not visibly improve generalization. Empirical hypothesis. In image classification, even with extensive label noise, large, deep neural networks with competitive test performance do not benefit from early stopping. Appendix F examines this empirical hypothesis in more detail. We report the unsmoothed neural network trajectories and training losses behind Figure 1 , together with additional convolutional and residual architectures. We also consider other training procedures commonly used to obtain stronger performance on image-classification tasks, combining cross-entropy loss, data augmentation, learning-rate warm-up and cosine decay, followed by an extended constant-rate tail. We also replace the automobiles by randomly labelled cats and dogs, so that clean and randomized examples belong to the same image classes. The evidence collected in Appendix F robustly points to the same qualitative behavior: the larger and more complex networks attain their best observed test performance after all random labels have been classified correctly, with little subsequent deterioration. Further controls examine the effects of the optimizer, batch size, training-set size and fraction of random labels. This raises the theoretical question of whether there are settings in which one can show analytically that training all the way to interpolation gives the lowest test error. This question is related to, but distinct from, grokking and benign overfitting. Canonical grokking concerns noiseless, realizable tasks, where training accuracy becomes essentially perfect long before test performance improves ( Power et al., 2022 ) . Here, instead, a considerable fraction of the labels is intrinsically unpredictable, and we ask whether fitting them eventually harms generalization. Benign overfitting asks whether an interpolating estimator can generalize well despite label noise ( Bartlett et al., 2020 ; Liang and Rakhlin, 2020 ) ; it does not by itself determine whether interpolation is optimal relative to earlier points along the training trajectory. Our focus is precisely on this dynamical comparison between early stopping and convergence. Can the minimum test error nevertheless genuinely occur at convergence? Existing theoretical analyses that follow feature-learning dynamics under label noise toward interpolation reach the opposite conclusion for the shallow neural networks they study in the regimes analyzed: fitting the noisy labels eventually degrades generalization, making early stopping preferable ( Han et al., 2025 ; Montanari and Urbani, 2025 ) . They therefore do not account for the empirical hypothesis formulated here. We show that such behavior is possible for square-loss kernel gradient flow in the Rules-and-Facts (RAF) model introduced by Farné et al. (2026) . Each training label either follows a shared linear rule or is independent of the input. Whereas Farné et al. (2026) analyze the resulting empirical risk minimizers (ERM) under explicit regularization, here we follow the full learning trajectory from initialization to interpolation in the absence of explicit regularization. In the proportional high-dimensional limit, this trajectory is governed by the relative strengths of the rule-aligned component and the higher-order kernel components that provide the capacity to fit the unpredictable labels. Main theoretical result. We derive exact learning curves and obtain a phase diagram with three regimes, corresponding to three families of kernels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. Thus, even in the presence of extensive label noise, interpolation can lead to a better test error than any early stopping. The kernel analysis therefore produces the behavior that motivated this work. At the critical geometry, the best test error is attained at interpolation, and the corresponding trajectory in Figure 4 closely resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 , whose best test performance is attained after all randomly labelled examples have been classified correctly. The theory thus provides a concrete realization of the observed phenomenon. It does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. Determining which aspects of feature learning, model size, and architecture produce this behavior remains an open question. Related work. Learning with label noise. Deep networks can fit arbitrary random labels ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , while often learning shared structure before memorizing individual samples ( Arpit et al., 2017 ) . This separation of time scales motivates early stopping as a method for improving robustness to label noise ( Li et al., 2020 ; Bai et al., 2021 ) . The severity of late-time overfitting, however, depends on model capacity and optimization, as illustrated by epoch-wise double descent ( Nakkiran et al., 2021 ; Heckel and Yilmaz, 2021 ) and by the weak overtraining observed in sufficiently overparameterized models ( Advani et al., 2020 ) . These works do not provide an exact criterion for when fitting the remaining label noise ceases to harm generalization. Early stopping and learning trajectories. For least squares, early stopping acts as a spectral regularizer ( Yao et al., 2007 ; Raskutti et al., 2014 ) , and the complete gradient-flow trajectory has an explicit matrix-exponential form ( Ali et al., 2019 ) . High-dimensional learning curves have been derived for linear, kernel, and Gaussian-covariate models ( Advani et al., 2020 ; Ghosh et al., 2022 ; Bodin and Macris, 2022 ) , including regimes in which training error decreases while test error remains essentially unchanged ( Ghosh et al., 2022 ) . Recent work also interprets early stopping through a transient spectral transition in an anisotropic linear model ( Coeurdoux et al., 2026 ) . These analyses do not characterize the transition between lowest test error at finite time and at convergence across kernels. Early stopping and explicit regularization. Early stopping, Tikhonov regularization and other spectral filters can attain comparable statistical rates ( Bauer et al., 2007 ; Yao et al., 2007 ; Raskutti et al., 2014 ; Celisse and Wahl, 2021 ; Hu and Lei, 2022 ) . For least-squares regression, Ali et al. (2019) compare gradient flow with ridge regression under the calibration λ ≍ 1 / t \lambda\asymp 1/t and obtain uniform constant-factor risk comparisons. More recent work shows that a finitely stopped gradient-descent iterate can be represented as a generalized, spectrally dependent ridge solution ( Sonthalia et al., 2024 ) , while high-dimensional and finite-sample comparisons demonstrate that optimally stopped gradient descent and optimally tuned scalar ridge need not attain the same risk ( Stark and Steinberger, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . Our setting makes this distinction fully explicit for classification error. Benign overfitting and kernel geometry. Benign-overfitting theory characterizes when an interpolating estimator can generalize well despite label noise ( Bartlett et al., 2020 ; Liang and Rakhlin, 2020 ) . More generally, kernel spectra and their alignment with the target control generalization ( Bordelon et al., 2020 ; Canatar et al., 2021 ; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2022 ) , while high-dimensional kernel linearization makes this dependence explicit for broad kernel families ( El Karoui, 2010 ; Do and Vu, 2013 ) . The RAF model provides a characterization of how kernel geometry allocates capacity between rule learning and fitting unpredictable labels ( Farné et al., 2026 ) . These results do not compare full learning trajectories across kernel geometries to determine when the test error at interpolation is lower than at every finite stopping time. 2 Data & kernel dynamics Synthetic data model. Figure 4 displays the analytical trajectories in the same coordinates as the neural-network trajectories in Figure 1 . The data distribution, sample ratio, and initialization are fixed, while we vary the kernel angle γ \gamma . We distinguish three regimes, corresponding to the following kernel families. • Rule-dominated kernels, γ > γ c ​ ( ε ) \gamma>\gamma_{m c}(\varepsilon) , generalization initially improves but eventually deteriorates as the randomly labelled examples are fitted, producing a finite optimal stopping time. • Fact-dominated kernels, γ < γ c ​ ( ε ) \gamma<\gamma_{m c}(\varepsilon) , the generalization error continues to decrease until interpolation, but the resulting predictor remains suboptimal relative to the critical kernel. • Optimal kernels, γ = γ c ​ ( ε ) \gamma=\gamma_{m c}(\varepsilon) : the trajectory reaches the lowest (among all considered kernels and stopping times) test error at the interpolating endpoint, where the memorization error vanishes. Thus, eliminating the benefit of early stopping is not sufficient: optimality is attained specifically at the boundary between the finite-time and interpolation-optimal regimes. All three kernel families have enough capacity to eventually interpolate the training data. What differs is how fitting the unpredictable labels affects predictions on new examples. The critical geometry provides a fixed-representation mechanism through which interpolation can be completed without sacrificing the best generalization attainable within the kernel family. Its trajectory qualitatively resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 . The kernel analysis does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties.
